title: Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads UTF-8 without BOM as ANSI and turns a valid script into a syntax error
title_zh: PowerShell 5.1 把无 BOM 的 UTF-8 当 ANSI 读，脚本整体语法错误
symptom: A script that looks correct in the editor fails at parse time with errors pointing at a line that plainly looks fine, e.g. `Unexpected token` / `字符串缺少终止符` / `Missing closing '}'`. Non-ASCII literals inside the script render as mojibake when the error is echoed back. The same file executes correctly on another machine or under PowerShell 7.
wrong_handling: Re-type the offending line, assuming a typo or an invisible character.
Switch editors or re-save the file as 'UTF-8' (many Windows editors mean UTF-8 *without* BOM, reproducing the bug exactly).
Bisect the script by deleting half of it, hunting for a logic error that does not exist.
Rewrite the script into another language to 'work around the encoding'.
Blame the terminal font or the console code page.
root_cause: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (the one shipped with the OS, `powershell.exe`) decodes a script file as the system ANSI code page (e.g. GBK/CP936 on zh-CN) unless the file starts with a UTF-8 BOM. A BOM-less UTF-8 file containing multi-byte characters is therefore mis-decoded: byte pairs of a CJK string are read as garbage characters, which can produce stray quote characters or braces and break tokenization of the *whole file*. The parser then reports errors far from the true origin. PowerShell 7+ defaults to UTF-8 and does not show the problem, which is why the same file 'works for someone else'.
correct_handling: Identify the interpreter: `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major` — 5 means this failure mode applies.
Check the first three bytes of the file; UTF-8 BOM is EF BB BF. If absent and the file contains non-ASCII, that is the cause.

Fix by choosing one of two shapes: (a) keep the script body pure ASCII, and move all non-ASCII text into a separate data file (JSON/UTF-8) loaded at runtime; or (b) save the script as UTF-8 **with BOM**.
Prefer (a) for scripts, because it is immune to the next editor that 'helpfully' strips the BOM.
Re-run and confirm the parse error is gone before touching anything else.
guardrail: Script bodies stay ASCII-only, or carry an explicit UTF-8 BOM. No exceptions.
Non-ASCII content lives in data files, never as string literals inside .ps1 source.
Any 'syntax error on a line that looks correct' in PowerShell 5.1 should route straight to an encoding check, before any logic debugging.
detection: `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.Major` to know whether the ANSI default applies.
Write a two-line probe script containing one CJK literal and see whether it parses.
evidence: Reproduced repeatedly on a zh-CN Windows host with an agent workspace that generates .ps1 files programmatically
